{{Short description|Analogy in fluid dynamics}}
The '''Reynolds Analogy''' is popularly known to relate turbulent momentum and heat transfer.<ref name=Gean>Geankoplis, C.J. ''Transport processes and separation process principles'' (2003), Fourth Edition, p. 475.</ref> That is because in a turbulent flow (in a pipe or in a [[boundary layer]]) the transport of momentum and the transport of heat largely depends on the same turbulent [[Eddy (fluid dynamics)|eddies]]: the velocity and the temperature profiles have the same shape. 

The main assumption is that wall [[heat flux]] <math>\dot{q}_w</math> in a turbulent system is analogous to momentum flux, or wall [[shear stress]], <math>\tau_w</math>, which suggests that the ratio <math>\frac{\tau_w}{\dot{q}_w}</math> must be constant for similar geometry. A common example for "similar geometry" is every radial position around a pipe at some [[Cross section (geometry)|cross-section]] with circular shape.

If the wall shear stress (<math>\tau_w</math>) is known, a relation for the turbulent heat flux (<math>\dot{q}_w</math>) can be found (or vice versa), making it a useful analogy for pipe flows and [[Hypersonic speed|hypersonic]] applications where <math>\tau_w</math> may be more easily estimated than <math>\dot{q}_w</math>.

This is often used to estimate wall heat flux on a body in a flow<ref>{{cite web |last1=Greitzer |first1=E. M. |last2=Spakovszky |first2=Z. S. |last3=Waitz |first3=I. A. |title=Thermodynamics and Propulsion Open Course Ware §17.1 |url=https://web.mit.edu/16.unified/www/FALL/thermodynamics/notes/node122.html |website=MIT Open Course Ware |publisher=MIT |access-date=22 July 2026}}</ref>:
:<math display="block"> \dot{q}_w \approx \frac{\tau_wc_p(T_w-T_{\infty})}{u_{\infty}} </math>
where:
* '''<math>T_w,T_{\infty}</math>''' are the temperatures of the wall and [[freestream]] (or bulk, depending on application), respectively;
* '''<math>c_p</math>''' is the [[specific heat capacity]] at constant pressure for the fluid;
* '''<math>u_{\infty}</math>''' is the [[freestream]] (or bulk, depending on application) fluid velocity.


The complete Reynolds analogy (in a form more often seen in relation to pipe flows) is:
:<math display="block"> \frac{f}{2} = \frac{h}{c_p G} = \frac{k'_c}{v_\text{avg}} </math>
where:
* '''<math>f</math>''' is the [[Fanning friction factor]];
* '''<math>h</math>''' is the [[heat transfer coefficient]];
* '''<math>c_p</math>''' is the [[specific heat]] at constant pressure;
* '''<math>G</math>''' is the [[mass velocity]] (mass flow rate per unit area).

Experimental data for gas streams agree approximately with above equation if the [[Schmidt number|Schmidt]] and [[Prandtl number|Prandtl (<math>Pr</math>)]] numbers are near 1.0 and only [[skin friction]] is present in flow past a flat plate or inside a pipe. When liquids are present and/or  [[form drag]] is present, the analogy is conventionally known to be invalid.<ref name=Gean/>

In 2008, the qualitative validity of Reynolds' analogy was re-visited for [[laminar flow]] of an [[incompressible fluid]] with variable [[dynamic viscosity]] (<math>\mu</math>)<ref name=Mah>Mahulikar, S.P., & Herwig, H., 'Fluid friction in incompressible laminar convection: Reynolds' analogy revisited for variable fluid properties,' ''European Physical Journal B: Condensed Matter & Complex Systems'', '''62(1)''', (2008), pp. 77-86.</ref>. It was shown that the inverse dependence of [[Reynolds number]] (<math>Re</math>) and [[skin friction]] coefficient (<math>C_f</math>) is the basis for the validity of the analogy in both constant and variable <math>\mu</math> flows. 

For <math>\mu = \text{const.}</math>, the analogy reduces to the popular form where the [[Stanton number]] (<math>C_h\text{ or }St</math>) increases with increasing <math>Re</math>. For variable <math>\mu</math>, it reduces to <math>C_h</math> increasing with decreasing <math>Re</math>.

This is represented by<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Cogo |first1=Michele |last2=Depieri |first2=Davide |last3=Bernardini |first3=Matteo |last4=Picano |first4=Francesco |title=On the Reynolds analogy for high-speed rough-wall flows: implications for wall modeling |journal=Journal of Fluid Mechanics |date=June 22, 2026 |volume=1039 |issue=A34 |pages=2-3 |doi=10.1017/jfm.2026.11842 |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/F3DEB9C3A63DBD4C75B85D7C9BBF9CD2/S0022112026118424a.pdf/on-the-reynolds-analogy-for-high-speed-rough-wall-flows-implications-for-wall-modelling.pdf |access-date=22 July 2026 |ref=PDF}}</ref>:
:<math display="block">s=\frac{2C_h}{C_f}\approx \text{constant}</math>
where:
* '''<math>s</math>''' is the Reynolds analogy factor which is coupled to the [[Prandtl number]] via <math>sPr\approx 0.8</math>;
* '''<math>C_f</math>''' is the skin friction coefficient given by <math>C_f=2\tau_w/(\rho_{\infty}u^2_{\infty})</math>;
** '''<math>\rho_{\infty}</math>''' is the [[freestream]] fluid density;
* '''<math>C_h</math>''' is the [[Stanton number]] (also often denoted <math>St</math>). In [[Supersonic speed|supersonic]]/[[Hypersonic speed|hypersonic]] applications, the Stanton Number is <math>C_h=\dot{q}_w/ (\rho_{\infty}u_{\infty}c_p(T_w-T_r))</math>;
** '''<math>T_r</math>''' is the recovery temperature, <math>T_r=T_{\infty}+Pr^{1/3}(\gamma-1)M^2_{\infty}/2</math>;
*** '''<math>\gamma</math>''' is the [[Heat capacity ratio|ratio of specific heats]], <math>\gamma=c_p/c_v</math>;
*** '''<math>M_{\infty}</math>''' is the freestream [[Mach number]].


Consequently, the [[Chilton and Colburn J-factor analogy|Chilton–Colburn analogy]] is qualitatively valid whenever the Reynolds' analogy is valid. Furthermore, the validity of the analogy is linked to the applicability of [[Prigogine's theorem|Prigogine's Theorem of Minimum Entropy Production]]<ref>Prigogine, I. ''Introduction to Thermodynamics of Irreversible Processes'' (1961), Interscience Publishers, New York.</ref>. Thus, Reynolds' analogy is valid for flows that are close to being [[Fluid dynamics#Developed flow|fully developed]], where changes in the gradients of velocity and temperature along the flow are small<ref name=Mah/>.
